But if you know how to add your own weight to the weight of nature, doubling the Mercury and tripling the sulfur, the work will be more quickly finished for the good, then for the better, and finally for the best; although there is only one apparent sulfur and two Mercuries, they are of one root. They should be neither raw nor over-cooked, yet purified and dissolved, if you have understood me.

    Indeed, there is no need to describe the matter of the Mercury of the Philosophers and the matter of their sulfur. No mortal has been able, nor will be able in the future, to describe it more openly and clearly than it has been described and named by the ancient Philosophers, unless he wishes to be an <term>anathema artis</term> <gloss>a curse or outsider to the art</gloss>. For it is so commonly named that it is not even esteemed; for this reason, seekers turn themselves toward other subtleties rather than remaining in the simplicity of nature. <summary>The author explains that while Mercury alone can perfect the work, adding specific proportions of sulfur accelerates the process toward perfection. He notes that the true materials of alchemy are plainly named by the ancients but are overlooked by many because of their perceived commonness.</summary>
<keywords>Mercury, sulfur, proportions, ancient Philosophers, simplicity of nature, alchemical matter</keywords>
